caseName: United States v. Columbia Falls Aluminum Company, LLC
citation: Consent Decree, U.S. District Court for the District of Montana (Missoula Division), lodged July 2026
court: U.S. District Court for the District of Montana
keyFacts: CFAC's former aluminum smelter in Columbia Falls, MT left arsenic, cyanide, fluoride, and polyaromatic hydrocarbon contamination in soil and groundwater. CFAC ceased smelting operations years before this settlement but remained the site's owner of record.
outcome: 647-page consent decree between EPA/Montana DEQ and CFAC requiring a $57.6 million cleanup, including a groundwater slurry wall and low-permeability landfill caps to stop contaminant migration toward the Flathead River. Open for public comment through Aug. 6, 2026.
dollarAmountBasis: Total consent decree cleanup cost disclosed in EPA press release
notes: Already tracked on CREdocket (live-019). Illustrates that Superfund liability attaches to the site/owner of record, not just an operating business — CFAC remained liable years after ceasing operations.

caseName: United States v. Alden Leeds, Inc., et al. (Lower Passaic River Study Area / Diamond Alkali Superfund Site)
citation: Consent Decree, D.N.J., approved and entered Dec. 18, 2024 (Judge Madeline Cox Arleo)
court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
keyFacts: 85 (later 82) potentially responsible parties held liable for discharging hazardous substances (dioxin, PCBs, heavy metals, pesticides) into the 17-mile tidal Lower Passaic River, part of the Diamond Alkali Superfund Site in Newark, NJ.
outcome: Consent decree requiring a $150 million collective payment toward EPA's past and anticipated future cleanup response costs; approved and entered by the district court Dec. 18, 2024.
dollarAmountBasis: Total collective payment by settling PRPs disclosed in DOJ/EPA press release
notes: One of the largest CERCLA cost-recovery consent decrees on record; illustrates multi-party cost allocation among dozens of PRPs for a large contaminated waterway adjoining industrial/commercial parcels.

caseName: United States v. NL Industries, Inc., et al. (Raritan Bay Slag Superfund Site)
citation: Proposed Consent Decree, D.N.J., lodged Sept. 5, 2024
court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
keyFacts: Slag from blast-furnace operations and battery casings (late 1960s-early 1970s) contaminated Raritan Bay's southern shore in Old Bridge and Sayreville, NJ with elevated lead levels, closing a recreational beach. NL Industries and its former customers are the primary settling defendants.
outcome: Proposed consent decree totaling $151.1 million: $132.4 million to reimburse EPA for past and future cleanup costs, plus $18.7 million to resolve natural resource damage claims.
dollarAmountBasis: Total settlement value disclosed in EPA press release ($132.4M cleanup reimbursement + $18.7M NRD)
notes: Combines CERCLA cost recovery and natural resource damages in a single settlement; useful benchmark for combined cleanup + NRD exposure at a large legacy industrial waterfront site.

caseName: United States v. Boeing Co., City of Seattle, and King County (Lower Duwamish Waterway Superfund Site)
citation: Settlement Agreement, W.D. Wash., announced March 2026
court: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington
keyFacts: A five-mile industrial stretch of Seattle's Duwamish River contaminated by decades of airplane manufacturing, timber, cement/brick manufacturing, steel mills, marine construction, and drum recycling. The Lower Duwamish Waterway Group (Boeing, City of Seattle, King County) is the lead PRP group among 100+ contributing parties.
outcome: $668 million settlement requiring the Group to design and perform the in-water cleanup remedy (dredging and capping), estimated to take at least 10 years; the Group will receive roughly $130 million from other PRPs and $140 million from federal agencies toward the total.
dollarAmountBasis: Total estimated cleanup cost disclosed in DOJ/EPA press release
notes: One of the largest disclosed Superfund cleanup-cost figures; illustrates cost-sharing between a small named PRP group and a much larger pool of contributing parties (100+) plus federal agencies.

caseName: United States v. [Omega Chemical Corp. Superfund Site 66-Company PRP Group]
citation: Consent Decree, C.D. Cal., entered Mar. 31, 2017
court: U.S. District Court for the Central District of California
keyFacts: A former chemical recycling facility in Whittier, CA created a three-mile groundwater contamination plume addressed by EPA's 2011 Record of Decision. Sixty-six companies settled as a group to fund the remedy.
outcome: Consent decree requiring the 66-company group to spend an estimated $70 million to install wells and operate a groundwater treatment system, plus reimburse EPA $8 million and California DTSC $70,000 for past cleanup costs (total settlement value ~$78 million).
dollarAmountBasis: Combined groundwater remedy cost estimate ($70M) plus EPA/state past-cost reimbursement (~$8.07M) per EPA/DOJ press release
notes: Large multi-party (66 PRP) group settlement including de minimis contributors alongside major responsible parties — a common structure for shared cost recovery among many historical waste generators.

caseName: United States v. OXY USA Inc. (Copper Basin Mining District Superfund Site)
citation: Two concurrent Consent Decrees, E.D. Tenn., announced Apr. 22, 2016
court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee
keyFacts: Historic copper mining in Polk County, TN left the Ocoee River and an associated watershed contaminated with metals-laden sediment and acid mine drainage. OXY USA Inc. (an Occidental Petroleum subsidiary) is successor in interest to the historic mining operators.
outcome: OXY USA agreed to spend approximately $40 million to clean up contaminated water and sediments in the Ocoee River and watershed, and to reimburse EPA approximately $10.8 million for past cleanup costs (total settlement value ~$50.8 million, publicized as "$50 million").
dollarAmountBasis: $40M remediation cost + $10.8M EPA past-cost reimbursement per EPA case summary
notes: Successor-liability example: a corporate successor held liable for cleanup decades after the original mining operations ceased, illustrating long-tail CERCLA exposure that follows corporate ownership chains.

caseName: United States v. Ford Motor Co. and Borough of Ringwood (Ringwood Mines/Landfill Superfund Site)
citation: Consent Decree, D.N.J.
court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
keyFacts: Ford Motor Co. and the Borough of Ringwood are PRPs for benzene, 1,4-dioxane, and lead contamination in groundwater and mine water at a former mine/landfill site that received auto-manufacturing paint sludge and waste.
outcome: Consent decree requiring Ford and the Borough to perform a final, targeted groundwater cleanup phase, estimated to cost $3.4 million.
dollarAmountBasis: Estimated final cleanup cost disclosed in DOJ press release
notes: A smaller-dollar, later-stage "final phase" consent decree — a useful counterpoint to the nine- and ten-figure settlements in this dataset, showing that not every Superfund consent decree is a mega-settlement.

caseName: United States v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (Anaconda Smelter Superfund Site)
citation: Consent Decree, D. Mont. (Butte Division), entered Dec. 16, 2022
court: U.S. District Court for the District of Montana
keyFacts: Decades of copper smelting by Atlantic Richfield's predecessor contaminated residential yards, upland soils, and left slag piles across Anaconda and Opportunity, MT in the Deer Lodge Valley, one of the longest-running Superfund cleanups (ongoing since the 1980s).
outcome: Consent decree requiring Atlantic Richfield to complete the remaining remedial work (estimated $83.1 million) and reimburse EPA/DOJ $48 million plus approximately $185,000 to the U.S. Forest Service for oversight.
dollarAmountBasis: Sum of $83.1M estimated remaining remedial-work cost + $48M EPA/DOJ cost reimbursement + $185,000 to US Forest Service, per DOJ/EPA press release
notes: Represents the "final phase" of a Superfund cleanup running more than three decades, illustrating the multi-decade total liability tail a single legacy industrial site can carry.

caseName: United States, Navajo Nation, and State of New Mexico v. United Nuclear Corp. (Northeast Church Rock Mine)
citation: No. 1:25-cv-00765 (D.N.M., consent decree lodged Aug. 2025)
court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico
keyFacts: A former uranium mine on Navajo Nation land near Gallup, NM left radioactive mine waste. United Nuclear Corp. and General Electric are the PRPs, with the Navajo Nation and State of New Mexico joining the United States as co-plaintiffs.
outcome: Consent decree requiring United Nuclear Corp. and GE to perform a nearly $63 million, decade-long cleanup of uranium mine waste.
dollarAmountBasis: Total disclosed cleanup cost per EPA/DOJ press release
notes: Notable for a tribal government (Navajo Nation) as co-plaintiff alongside federal and state government; radioactive mining contamination rather than typical commercial contamination, but a real, disclosed cleanup-cost figure tied to real property remediation liability.

caseName: United States, et al. v. Pharmacia Corp. and Bayer CropScience Inc. (Industri-Plex Superfund Site NRD Settlement)
citation: Consent Decree, D. Mass., lodged 2012, defendants paid settlement in 2013
court: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts
keyFacts: Industrial operations from the 1850s to 1960s (pesticides, munitions, leather, glue manufacturing) by Stauffer Chemical Co. and Merrimac Chemical Co. (predecessors to Pharmacia Corp. and Bayer CropScience Inc.) contaminated the Aberjona River, wetlands, and Mystic Lakes with arsenic and chromium in Woburn, MA.
outcome: Defendants paid $4.25 million to federal and state natural resource trustees to resolve natural resource damage claims; approximately $3.8 million funded wetland, stream, and pond habitat restoration.
dollarAmountBasis: Total natural resource damages settlement amount disclosed in DOJ/USFWS press release
notes: A pure natural-resource-damages settlement (separate from the site's much larger underlying cleanup-cost history), useful as a benchmark for NRD-only exposure distinct from remediation cost itself.

caseName: United States and State of New Jersey v. PPG Industries, Inc. (Riverside Industrial Park Superfund Site)
citation: Proposed Consent Decree, D.N.J., announced Apr. 16, 2024
court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
keyFacts: PPG Industries' predecessor operated a paint and varnish manufacturing facility (1902-1971) at 29 Riverside Avenue in Newark, NJ on the Passaic River, leaving lead-contaminated soil and a deteriorated riverbank bulkhead across the 7.6-acre site.
outcome: Consent decree requiring PPG to design and perform remediation (estimated $15.8 million: excavation, bulkhead reinforcement, capping, vapor intrusion mitigation, groundwater monitoring) plus reimburse EPA $2.9 million and NJDEP $117,000 for past costs (total nearly $19 million).
dollarAmountBasis: $15.8M cleanup design/performance cost + $2.9M EPA reimbursement + $117,000 NJDEP reimbursement per EPA press release
notes: Single-defendant (not multi-party group) consent decree; a useful benchmark for a mid-size legacy manufacturing site with one clearly identified responsible party.

caseName: New Jersey Dep't of Environmental Protection v. Solvay Specialty Polymers USA, LLC
citation: Proposed Judicial Consent Order, NJ state enforcement action (West Deptford PFAS matter)
court: New Jersey state court / NJDEP enforcement action
keyFacts: Solvay's West Deptford, NJ facility used a PFOA/PFNA-containing process aid ("Surflon") for more than 30 years, contaminating a roughly 37-mile area of groundwater and surface water in southern New Jersey with PFAS ("forever chemicals").
outcome: Proposed Judicial Consent Order: Solvay to pay $75 million for natural resource damages, $100 million to fund NJDEP-directed PFAS remediation projects in the area, and post $214 million in financial assurance to guarantee completion of its own ongoing remediation obligations (total $393 million).
dollarAmountBasis: Sum of $75M NRD + $100M remediation project funding + $214M financial-assurance guarantee, per NJ Attorney General/DEP press release
notes: One of the largest state-level (non-federal-CERCLA) PFAS cleanup settlements in the country; illustrates emerging-contaminant (PFAS) exposure as a distinct and rapidly growing category from legacy CERCLA metals/solvent contamination.

caseName: Trinity Industries, Inc. v. Greenlease Holding Co.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit (appeal from W.D. Pa.)
keyFacts: Trinity Industries purchased a former railcar manufacturing and repair facility in Greenville, PA in 1986 and sold it in 2004; contamination (heavy metals, volatile organic compounds) surfaced afterward and Trinity spent approximately $9 million remediating it, then sued prior owner/operator Greenlease Holding Co. (a former Ampco-Pittsburgh subsidiary) for contribution.
outcome: The district court allocated 62% of the $9 million cleanup cost to Greenlease and 38% to Trinity under CERCLA Section 113(f). The Third Circuit affirmed the parent-subsidiary/operator liability findings (applying United States v. Bestfoods) while addressing related allocation issues.
dollarAmountBasis: Total remediation cost at issue in the contribution allocation, per Third Circuit opinion and secondary case summaries
notes: Leading appellate precedent on parent-corporation CERCLA "operator" liability; the 62%/38% allocation is a real-world example of a court-ordered contribution split between two former owners of the same industrial parcel.

caseName: Barclay Lofts LLC v. PPG Industries, Inc.
court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin
keyFacts: A developer bought two contaminated industrial parcels in Milwaukee's Walker's Point neighborhood in 2017 for $500,000 (reduced from a $2 million asking price because of hexavalent chromium, arsenic, mercury, lead, and trichloroethylene contamination) and sued a chain of former owners/operators spanning 1905-2017, including PPG Industries and Hydrite Chemical.
outcome: Court awarded $1.17 million of $1.43 million in past response costs claimed, and allocated future response-cost shares: PPG 50%, Hydrite 20%, an unrecoverable "orphan share" of 20% assigned to plaintiff, Barclay/Sherman 10%, and 0% each to two other defendants. Hydrite separately settled for $550,000 (past costs) plus a $3 million escrow (future costs).
dollarAmountBasis: Past response costs actually recovered by court order, per case summary; future-cost estimates ranged from $6.7M (defense expert) to over $28M (plaintiff's experts) and were allocated by percentage rather than a fixed dollar figure
notes: Detailed 2024 CERCLA equitable-factor (Gore factor) allocation across six PRPs spanning over a century of site ownership; the wide gap between competing future-cost estimates ($6.7M vs. $28M+) is itself a useful data point on remediation-cost uncertainty in contribution litigation.

caseName: Walnut Creek Manor, LLC v. Mayhew Center, LLC
citation: No. 4:07-cv-05664-CW (N.D. Cal.); related appeal GP Vincent II v. Estate of Beard, No. 21-16555 (9th Cir. May 17, 2023)
court: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California; U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
keyFacts: PCE (tetrachloroethylene) solvent contamination migrated from the Mayhew Center property to neighboring Walnut Creek Manor's land. Walnut Creek Manor sued under CERCLA to recover remediation costs; Mayhew in turn sued its own prior owner, Norma Beard, for contribution.
outcome: A jury awarded Walnut Creek Manor $350,000 in past damages and $1,597,000 in future damages ($1,947,000 total) against Mayhew; the district court held Mayhew 100% liable for future response costs. A successor entity, GP Vincent II, later pursued a related CERCLA cost-recovery claim against the Beard estate; the Ninth Circuit reversed a claim-preclusion dismissal in 2023 and remanded for further proceedings.
dollarAmountBasis: Sum of $350,000 past damages + $1,597,000 future damages jury verdict against Mayhew
notes: Illustrates the extended litigation tail of CERCLA contribution disputes: an initial cost-recovery suit produced a jury verdict, which triggered a second contribution suit against a still-earlier owner, which then produced a third cost-recovery suit by a later purchaser — spanning more than 15 years (2007-2023+).

caseName: Fox Investments LLC v. City of Kaukauna, et al.
citation: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin (filed 2024)
court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin
keyFacts: Fox Shore Apartments (400 Fox Shores Drive) sits on land the City of Kaukauna operated as a railyard from 1967-1974. A 2018 Phase II environmental site assessment found heavy metals and PAH constituents exceeding state standards, prompting Fox Investments to sue the city and three of its historical insurers (Sentry, Travelers Indemnity Co., Employers Insurance Co. of Wausau) directly under Wisconsin's direct-action statute.
outcome: Fox seeks recovery of $235,683.63 in investigation and remediation costs already incurred, pursuing the insurers directly on CERCLA cost recovery, negligence, and unjust enrichment theories rather than filing separate coverage litigation against the city first.
dollarAmountBasis: Investigation and remediation costs incurred by plaintiff, as pled in the complaint
notes: Illustrates a common "long-tail" environmental fact pattern: decades-old (1960s-70s) contamination surfacing only after a modern Phase II assessment, with the current owner suing the historical polluter's insurers directly under a state direct-action statute rather than the (often less collectible) government polluter itself.

caseName: Regency Centers Corp. v. Indian Harbor Insurance Co.
citation: No. 3:24-cv-00428 (M.D. Fla.), ruling issued May 7, 2026
court: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida
keyFacts: A Regency Centers-owned California shopping center was contaminated by chemicals from a former dry-cleaning tenant. Regency sought coverage from Indian Harbor Insurance Co. for remediation costs under a pollution/environmental liability policy.
outcome: The court ruled Indian Harbor owed no coverage, finding the insurer properly denied the claim under the policy's site-development and pollution exclusions.
dollarAmountBasis: Underlying remediation cost / claim amount not disclosed in available reporting; only the coverage-denial ruling is documented
notes: A coverage-denial outcome (rather than a dollar recovery) is a common real-world result in dry-cleaner/legacy-contamination coverage disputes, where site-development and pollution exclusions frequently defeat coverage even under a specialty environmental policy.

caseName: Travelers Property Casualty Co. of America and St. Paul Fire and Marine Ins. Co. v. Washington Shoppes LP and The Broadbent Co.
citation: No. 49D01-2511-CE-056363 (Marion Superior Court, Ind., filed Nov. 26, 2025)
court: Marion Superior Court, Indiana
keyFacts: Sunrise Dry Cleaners operated at an Indianapolis shopping center from 1987-1996; subsequent testing found PCE and its breakdown byproducts in soil and groundwater. Insurers filed a declaratory judgment action against the shopping center owner and property owner seeking a ruling that pollution-exclusion clauses bar coverage for remediation.
outcome: Case pending as of the research date (filed Nov. 26, 2025); insurers seek a declaration of no coverage obligation and separately dispute whether the owner qualifies as an insured and whether contamination predated the relevant policy periods.
dollarAmountBasis: Remediation cost amount not disclosed in the complaint as reported
notes: Already tracked on CREdocket (live-017). Insurers here moved proactively/pre-emptively to disclaim coverage before being sued for it, rather than waiting for a coverage claim — a notable pattern distinct from the reactive Regency Centers case above.

caseName: New Jersey Dep't of Environmental Protection v. Sigma Realty, Inc.
citation: NJDEP civil enforcement action, filed 2022, settled 2025 (Ewing Township, Mercer County, NJ)
court: Superior Court of New Jersey (NJDEP administrative/civil enforcement)
keyFacts: Sigma Realty and its owners acquired a former gas station in Ewing, NJ in 1993 and failed for more than two decades to remediate known petroleum contamination, despite a 2020 NJDEP Administrative Order and Notice of Civil Administrative Penalty Assessment (which itself included a $105,000 penalty).
outcome: After selling the property to a third party in July 2025 (who separately agreed with NJDEP to complete remediation and pay outstanding fees), Sigma Realty and its owners paid a $117,500 civil penalty to resolve the enforcement lawsuit.
dollarAmountBasis: Total civil penalty paid to resolve the enforcement lawsuit, per NJ Attorney General press release
notes: Small-property, non-CERCLA example: a state Spill Act enforcement civil penalty (not itself a full cleanup-cost figure) against a small commercial (gas station) owner who let contamination sit unremediated for roughly 25+ years — illustrates the lower end of real-world environmental enforcement dollar exposure, in contrast to the nine-figure federal Superfund settlements in this dataset.

caseName: New Jersey Dep't of Environmental Protection v. Estate of Kenneth Knapp / Solomon Dwek (Chatsworth Deli site)
citation: NJDEP civil enforcement action, Woodland Township, Burlington County, NJ
court: Superior Court of New Jersey (NJDEP administrative/civil enforcement)
keyFacts: A former gas station/deli site in Woodland Township, NJ (operated until the 1970s) left soil and groundwater contamination from leaking underground storage tanks, unremediated for decades in violation of the Spill Compensation and Control Act and Brownfield and Contaminated Site Remediation Act.
outcome: $85,000 civil administrative penalty docketed as a judgment against the Knapp estate/heirs.
dollarAmountBasis: Civil administrative penalty amount, per NJ Attorney General press release
notes: Another small-dollar state underground-storage-tank/gas-station enforcement penalty; useful for showing the low end of the state_cleanup_consent_decree dollar-figure range in this dataset.

caseName: People of the State of California v. Bay Area/Diablo Petroleum Co. (dba Golden Gate Petroleum), et al.
citation: Civil complaint filed 2018; settlement announced Mar. 6, 2023 (Northern California)
court: California state court (Attorney General/district attorney civil enforcement)
keyFacts: Five gas station owners/operators (Bay Area/Diablo Petroleum dba Golden Gate Petroleum, Westgate Petroleum Co., Eastgate Petroleum LLC, and owner Dennis O'Keefe) committed 107 violations of California's above-ground/underground storage tank and hazardous waste laws across 14 Northern California gas stations since at least 2013, including failing to maintain leak-detection and spill-containment systems.
outcome: $1.7 million settlement requiring civil penalties plus employment of an environmental compliance coordinator and ongoing annual compliance reporting.
dollarAmountBasis: Total settlement/penalty amount disclosed in California Attorney General press release
notes: Multi-site (14 gas stations) state enforcement settlement illustrating aggregated penalty exposure across a chain of commercial fuel-retail properties with systemic underground-storage-tank compliance failures, rather than a single contaminated site.
